questions.stem: In ED at night you are examining a 12 kg 2-year-old with 2 days of coryza, then a barking cough, hoarse cry and stridor at rest. The child is sitting upright on the mother's lap and is consolable. How should you carry out your examination?
options: Observe from a distance on mother's lap, counting RR and looking for recession and tug
Lie the child supine on the couch to auscultate the chest and look for recession and tug
Inspect the oropharynx with a tongue depressor and torch to exclude epiglottitis
Ask the nurse to take a capillary blood gas first to judge the severity objectively
questions.why: In croup, being upset makes the dynamic obstruction worse. Assess behaviour, stridor and work of breathing by watching, with the child upright and calm on the parent's lap. Do as little hands-on examination as you can.
notes: Lying the child flat and handling them upsets them and makes the airway obstruction worse. The station shows this: the stridor gets much louder.
Never examine the throat in a child with stridor. Distress worsens the obstruction, and in epiglottitis a tongue depressor can cause complete obstruction.
Croup is diagnosed and graded clinically. A blood gas does not change management and the needle upsets the child, which worsens the obstruction.

questions.stem: At 23:00 the same 12 kg 2-year-old with croup is agitated with loud stridor at rest, marked recession, tracheal tug, RR 52 and SpO2 91% in room air. No medicines have been given yet. Dexamethasone has been charted and a senior is coming. Which adrenaline order is right for this child?
options: Adrenaline 1:1000, 0.5 mL diluted to 5 mL with saline, nebulised
Adrenaline 1:1000, 0.12 mL (0.01 mg/kg) intramuscularly into the lateral thigh
Adrenaline 1:1000, 5 mL undiluted, nebulised via an oxygen-driven mask
Adrenaline 1:10 000, 1.2 mL (0.01 mg/kg) intravenously over 1 minute
questions.why: For severe croup, give nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL), 5 mL undiluted (0.5 mL/kg, capped at 5 mL, so 5 mL for 12 kg). Run it on oxygen because SpO2 is under 92%. It works within minutes but lasts about 2 hours, so observe for at least 3 hours after the last dose.
notes: 0.5 mL is only a tenth of the croup dose. That is a racemic-adrenaline regimen, not the Australian 1:1000 regimen of 5 mL undiluted.
IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg treats anaphylaxis. This child has no allergic features, and croup is treated with nebulised adrenaline acting directly on the laryngeal mucosa.
IV adrenaline is a cardiac arrest or peri-arrest drug. It has no role in croup and puts the child at risk of arrhythmias and severe hypertension.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with croup has loud stridor that is mainly inspiratory and gets worse when the child cries and breathes in hard. What is the main reason the stridor in croup is heard mostly on inspiration?
options: In inspiration, positive pleural pressure compresses the narrowed intrathoracic trachea
In inspiration, extrathoracic airway pressure falls below atmospheric pressure
In inspiration, the vocal cords adduct, narrowing the glottis that is already swollen
In inspiration, small-airway bronchospasm traps air and creates turbulent flow
questions.why: The subglottic narrowing in croup is outside the chest. On inspiration, pressure inside the lumen falls below atmospheric pressure, so the swollen extrathoracic airway is pulled narrower and flow becomes turbulent. Hard breathing when the child is upset makes this worse.
notes: Pleural pressure is negative during inspiration. Intrathoracic airways are compressed in forced expiration, which is why intrathoracic obstruction gives expiratory noise.
The vocal cords abduct during inspiration, opening the glottis. They do not adduct.
Bronchospasm of the small airways causes expiratory wheeze, as in asthma. It does not cause inspiratory stridor from upper airway oedema.

questions.stem: The mother of a 2-year-old with croup asks why a simple cold has made breathing so hard. You explain that croup causes inflammatory swelling just below the vocal cords, inside a rigid ring that cannot stretch outward. Which structure forms this ring?
options: Thyroid cartilage, at the level of the vocal cords
First tracheal ring, just below the larynx
Cricoid cartilage, just below the vocal cords
questions.why: The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway, and it surrounds the subglottis. Mucosal oedema there can only narrow the lumen inward. Airway resistance rises steeply as the radius falls, so in a toddler a little swelling causes marked obstruction.
notes: The thyroid cartilage is open at the back and sits at glottic level. It does not form a complete ring around the subglottis, where croup swelling is greatest.
The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap above the glottis. It is the swollen structure in epiglottitis, not in croup.
Tracheal rings are C-shaped and open at the back, closed only by the trachealis muscle, so they are not complete rigid rings.
